summary: Bank of Algeria banned cash deposits into commercial accounts from 23 Dec 2025 to force traceability.
implication: Distributors and SMEs that collect cash from retail had to shift to cheques/transfers; expect slower payment cycles from distributors in 2026.

summary: BoA note of 4 Jan 2026 allows commercial accounts to be funded by scriptural means or cash in line with daily/weekly turnover and client profile; governor replaced by interim Mouatassem Boudiaf the same day.
implication: Cash remains usable for turnover-linked deposits; policy is volatile, so do not build a credit policy on one rule.

summary: Algérie Eco/ObservAlgérie describe a one-month transition with decreasing cash deposits, then cash deposits banned again end-Jan 2026 except rare justified cases; conflicts with TSA/APS framing of a lift.
implication: Status after Jan 2026 UNKNOWN; ask each buyer how they pay now.

summary: Small retailers pay distributors in cash; distributors deposit cash then pay manufacturers/importers by cheque or transfer.
implication: A molder selling to distributors will mostly be paid by cheque/transfer funded by retail cash; distributor liquidity is the real credit risk.

summary: Fewer than 80,000 TPE for more than 2 million merchants up to end-April 2025; rush to TPE after cash ban.
implication: Electronic B2B payment is immature; cheques and traites remain the B2B instruments.

summary: Cash banned for property, dealer vehicle sales, yachts and mandatory insurance; ordinary B2B goods not listed.
implication: No legal obligation found that forces B2B plastic-part buyers off cash below the scriptural threshold.

summary: Algérie360: scriptural payment to become mandatory above 500,000 DA; business community opposed the cheque push.
implication: Current threshold not verified (background knowledge suggests 1,000,000 DA later); verify before invoicing policy.

summary: Issuing a cheque without provision is a délit under Penal Code arts 374-375; Commercial Code arts 538-539 abrogated and redirected to the penal code.
implication: Criminal sanction gives the creditor leverage; keep invoices and BL to use it.

summary: BoA Regulation 08-01: banks consult the Centrale des impayés before issuing chequebooks; incident declared within 4 working days; one free regularisation per year within 10 days, else 5-year cheque ban.
implication: Ask your bank to check a buyer's cheque status before granting credit.

summary: Centrale des impayés recorded 64,699 cheque incidents worth 99.4 bn DA at end-2016, sharply up on 2015.
implication: Bounced-cheque risk is material; provision for it and prefer certified cheques or avalised traites. No post-2016 data found.

summary: Bounced cheques taking 'worrying proportions'; users see cheques as unsecured; few institutions use BoA security device.
implication: Ordinary cheques on credit are risky for a new supplier; demand certified cheques for first orders.

summary: Searches found Tunisia (2024-25) and Morocco (2025-26) reforms but no Algerian decriminalisation or amnesty.
implication: Assume the penal regime still applies; confirm with a lawyer/bank.

summary: Construction contractors claimed 130 bn DA of unpaid public receivables; PM allowed firms to defer taxes pending collection.
implication: Precast/construction buyers dependent on public projects pass delays down the chain; limit credit to them.

summary: About 35,000 BTP contractors still awaiting dues despite >60 bn DA government injection.
implication: Same as above; ask construction buyers who their end client is.

summary: ENIEM: raw-material stockouts, no bank credit for supplies, full stop 2023, unpaid wages, ~5 bn DA debt.
implication: Advance payment only for distressed public buyers.

summary: BoA Regulation 26-03 (JO n°67) sets conditions for banks/financial institutions to do factoring.
implication: Factoring may become a way to finance receivables from groups, but not yet a market product; revisit in 2027.

summary: Afreximbank/FCI factoring workshop at IATF 2025 Algiers under BoA auspices (~100 participants).
implication: Factoring culture is nascent.

summary: Half of operators' revenue said to come from informal economy; sales without invoices ~155 bn DA over 3 years; wholesalers refuse invoices with retailers; formal firms pushed to sell without invoice.
implication: Expect requests to sell 'sans facture'; refuse credit to such buyers; formal buyers needing VAT invoices are the safer segment.

summary: Algerian SME research: centralised decision-making by the owner-founder is a defining trait of the family SME.
implication: Sell to the owner/gérant in SMEs; the owner also controls payment.

product_or_topic: Formal supplier scoring in a public group
summary: Cosider Canalisations purchasing used AHP supplier selection on quality, delivery time, cost, financial health.
implication: Groups score delivery and financial health, not only price; prepare a supplier file with capacity and finances.

summary: Arabic case study applies AHP to supplier selection at Sonelgaz (east).
implication: Large public firms use formal multi-criteria evaluation.

summary: Univers Détergent recruits a junior acheteur technique to analyse technical needs with departments, select/negotiate suppliers, follow delivery and quality.
implication: Mid-size detergent firms have a buyer who screens suppliers; technical needs come from production.

summary: Biaxial Films Packaging (Sétif) seeks buyer 6-10 yrs Bac+5; MCE (Boumerdès) and Vital Care also recruit buyers.
implication: Formal purchasing exists in mid/large firms; target purchasing plus QA.

summary: Henkel Algérie: ~7/10 inputs local; all packaging from Algerian workshops, some inside the Réghaïa complex ('wall-to-wall'); target 2/3 local raw-material packaging; ~70% integration.
implication: Multinationals actively develop local suppliers; closeness to plant is a selection criterion.

summary: Public-company managers are 'frileux' about national subcontractors; foreign firms win contracts.
implication: Public buyers are hard first customers; private SMEs and multinationals with integration targets are easier.

summary: Subcontracting described as embryonic; officials call for a true relationship of trust between large contractors and local subcontractors.
implication: Trust must be built by demonstrable capacity, samples and references.

summary: Since April 2022 imports need Algex approval that goods are not sufficiently produced locally; cereal sector lacks inputs and spare parts.
implication: Import controls create availability-driven switching to local suppliers, especially for spare parts.

summary: Car spare parts increasingly rare; buying them is a 'parcours du combattant'.
implication: Maintenance and spare-part buyers value availability over price.

summary: Executive Decree 25-170 legalises cabas: individuals may import goods for resale up to 1.8M DA per trip, twice a month. (Corrects Phase 1, which tied 25-170 to the PPI.)
implication: Cabas is a legal backup channel for small high-value parts; a local molder must beat it on volume, bulk, custom fit and invoice.

summary: Cabas trade estimated at USD 2-3 bn per year; items include auto spare parts.
implication: Informal import is a real competitor for small parts; ask buyers if they use it (interview Q2).

summary: Imports must be domiciled before shipment with a 120% provision at least 30 days ahead (BoA Note 01/DGC/2026).
implication: Raises cash cost and lead time of imported parts, so buyers have more reason to switch to local stock.

summary: No Algerian source found on who pays for molds (customer vs molder); international norm is customer-funded, customer-owned.
implication: Offer three options (customer-funded, shared/amortised, molder-owned stock mold); ask interview Q14-15.

product_or_topic: B2B credit days, trial orders, switching
summary: No survey on 30/60/90-day terms, DSO, trial-order sizes or switching rates in Algerian industry; WB Enterprise Survey Algeria last round 2007.
implication: Run 20+ behavioral interviews before setting credit policy.
